analysis.title: How high can yields go before equities break?
key_insights: JPM argues the S&P 500 may be more resilient to higher Treasury yields than investors assume. With consensus EPS growth above 20%, JPM sees the index potentially tolerating 10-year yields of about 5.5-6%.
The key variable is whether earnings keep delivering, not the level of rates alone. When earnings growth is strong, stocks can absorb substantially higher rates before valuations come under pressure.

Stronger productivity growth can support higher equity multiples even as bond yields rise. AI could lift corporate efficiency, but the gains have to show up in actual earnings and not only in expectations.

JPM estimates roughly 91% of S&P 500 nonfinancial debt is fixed-rate. This delays the effect of higher yields on corporate earnings, and the pressure is concentrated in businesses that need fresh capital.

Curve shape matters alongside the level of rates. Bear steepeners have historically favored cyclicals such as Energy and Financials, and bear flatteners have been more supportive of Technology. Bond proxies and long-duration sectors outside tech are the most vulnerable.

AI financing is split. JPM estimates CoreWeave's debt costs 8-9%. Oracle's FY27 capex plan of $90-95bn implies about $70bn of net cash spending after funding offsets. Higher rates raise the cost of new capacity and pressure project returns.
SPY has held up with 10-year yields around 5%, while IWM has struggled considerably more. JPM favors large-cap Quality Growth over smaller, more financing-sensitive companies.
A shallow hiking cycle may be manageable for the index. A broader tightening cycle could increasingly favor defensive low volatility exposure.
